questions.q: What did the four men do who were carrying the paralyzed man?
questions.a: The men removed the roof of the house and lowered the paralyzed man to Jesus.

questions.q: What did Jesus say to the paralyzed man?
questions.a: Jesus said, “Child, your sins are forgiven.”

questions.q: Why did some of the scribes object to what Jesus had said?
questions.a: Some of the scribes reasoned that Jesus had blasphemed because only God can forgive sins.

questions.q: How did Jesus demonstrate that he had authority on earth to forgive sins?
questions.a: Jesus told the paralyzed man to take up his bed and go to his house, and the man did.

questions.q: What was Levi doing when Jesus told Levi to follow him?
questions.a: Levi was sitting at the tax-collecting place when Jesus called him.

questions.q: At Levi’s house, what was Jesus doing that offended the Pharisees?
questions.a: Jesus was dining with the sinful people and tax collectors.

questions.q: Who did Jesus say he had come to call?
questions.a: Jesus said he had come to call sinful people.

questions.q: What question did some people ask Jesus about fasting?
questions.a: They asked Jesus why his disciples did not fast when John’s disciples and the Pharisees’ disciples did fast.

questions.q: How did Jesus explain why his disciples were not fasting?
questions.a: Jesus said that while the bridegroom is still with the wedding attendants, they cannot fast.

questions.q: What did Jesus’ disciples do in some fields on the Sabbath which offended the Pharisees?
questions.a: Jesus’ disciples picked heads of grain and ate them on the Sabbath.

questions.q: What example did Jesus give of someone who needed and ate bread normally forbidden for them?
questions.a: Jesus gave the example of David who, out of need, ate the bread of the presence, normally reserved for the priests.

questions.q: For whom did Jesus say the Sabbath was made?
questions.a: Jesus said the Sabbath was made for people.

questions.q: What authority did Jesus claim for himself?
questions.a: Jesus said that he was Lord also of the Sabbath.

commentary.text: Christ heals one sick of the palsy.
Levi's call, and the entertainment given to Jesus.
Why Christ's disciples did not fast.
He justifies his disciples for plucking corn on the sabbath.

Verses 1–12 It was this man's misery that he needed to be so carried, and shows the suffering state of human life; it was kind of those who so carried him, and teaches the compassion that should be in men, toward their fellow-creatures in distress. True faith and strong faith may work in various ways; but it shall be accepted and approved by Jesus Christ. Sin is the cause of all our pains and sicknesses. The way to remove the effect, is to take away the cause. Pardon of sin strikes at the root of all diseases. Christ proved his power to forgive sin, by showing his power to cure the man sick of the palsy. And his curing diseases was a figure of his pardoning sin, for sin is the disease of the soul; when it is pardoned, it is healed. When we see what Christ does in healing souls, we must own that we never saw the like. Most men think themselves whole; they feel no need of a physician, therefore despise or neglect Christ and his gospel. But the convinced, humbled sinner, who despairs of all help, excepting from the Saviour, will show his faith by applying to him without delay.

Matthew was not a good character, or else, being a Jew, he would never have been a publican, that is, a tax-gatherer for the Romans. However, Christ called this publican to follow him. With God, through Christ, there is mercy to pardon the greatest sins, and grace to change the greatest sinners, and make them holy. A faithful, fair-dealing publican was rare. And because the Jews had a particular hatred to an office which proved that they were subject to the Romans, they gave these tax-gatherers an ill name. But such as these our blessed Lord did not hesitate to converse with, when he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh. And it is no new thing for that which is both well done and well designed, to be slandered, and turned to the reproach of the wisest and best of men. Christ would not withdraw, though the Pharisees were offended. If the world had been righteous, there had been no occasion for his coming, either to preach repentance, or to purchase forgiveness. We must not keep company with ungodly men out of love to their vain conversation; but we are to show love to their souls, remembering that our good Physician had the power of healing in himself, and was in no danger of taking the disease; but it is not so with us. In trying to do good to others, let us be careful we do not get harm to ourselves.

Strict professors are apt to blame all that do not fully come up to their own views. Christ did not escape slanders; we should be willing to bear them, as well as careful not to deserve them; but should attend to every part of our duty in its proper order and season.

The sabbath is a sacred and Divine institution; a privilege and benefit, not a task and drudgery. God never designed it to be a burden to us, therefore we must not make it so to ourselves. The sabbath was instituted for the good of mankind, as living in society, having many wants and troubles, preparing for a state of happiness or misery. Man was not made for the sabbath, as if his keeping it could be of service to God, nor was he commanded to keep it outward observances to his real hurt. Every observance respecting it, is to be interpreted by the rule of mercy.
